micros.title: Making a Thousand
micros.description: Bundle 10 hundreds into 1 thousand and count in thousands: 1000, 2000, ... 9000. The thousands place is the new fourth seat on the place-value mat.
outcomes: Can explain that 10 hundreds make 1 thousand
Can count in thousands from 1000 to 9000

micros.title: Reading and Writing 4-digit Numbers
micros.description: Turn number words into figures and back, using a Th | H | T | O mat. A zero must hold any empty place so the other digits stay in their seats.
outcomes: Can write a 4-digit number from its number name, including zero-rich ones like 4056
Can read any 4-digit number aloud correctly

question.prompt: Write 'four thousand and fifty-six' in figures.

options.diagnosis: Wrote the words down literally: 4000 then 56, glued together.
Dropped the zero that must hold the empty hundreds place.
The zero drifted — it must hold the hundreds, and the 5 sits in the tens.

question.explanation: 4 thousands, 0 hundreds, 5 tens, 6 ones — the zero holds the hundreds seat, giving 4056.

micros.title: Place Value and Expanded Form
micros.description: Every digit has a face and a value: the 5 in 2593 is worth 500 because it sits in the hundreds seat. Writing 2593 = 2000 + 500 + 90 + 3 shows each digit's true worth.
outcomes: Can state the place value of any digit in a 4-digit number
Can write a 4-digit number in expanded form and put expanded parts back together

question.prompt: What is the VALUE of the digit 5 in 2593?

options.diagnosis: Gave the face value and ignored the hundreds seat it sits in.
Placed the 5 one seat too far right — that would be the tens.
Placed the 5 one seat too far left — that would be the thousands.

question.explanation: In 2593 the 5 sits in the hundreds place, so it is worth 5 × 100 = 500. Expanded: 2000 + 500 + 90 + 3.

micros.title: Comparing and Ordering 4-digit Numbers
micros.description: Compare from the LEFT: thousands first, then hundreds, tens, ones. Shiny big digits on the right cannot beat one extra thousand on the left.
outcomes: Can compare two 4-digit numbers using > and <
Can put three or four 4-digit numbers in order

question.prompt: Which number is the GREATEST: 5999, 6100 or 6099?

options.diagnosis: Dazzled by the three 9s — but thousands are compared first.
Compared the last digits (9 beats 0) instead of working left to right.

options.text: They are all equal — each has 4 digits
options.diagnosis: Same number of digits does not mean same value; compare place by place.

question.explanation: Thousands first: 6100 and 6099 both have 6 thousands, beating 5999. Then hundreds: 1 beats 0, so 6100 is greatest.

micros.title: 1, 10, 100 or 1000 More or Less
micros.description: Jump up or down by 1, 10, 100 or 1000 from any 4-digit number — only one place changes, unless the jump rolls over into the next place.
outcomes: Can find 1, 10, 100 or 1000 more or less than a given number
Can handle jumps that cross over, like 100 more than 3950

question.prompt: What is 100 more than 3950?

options.diagnosis: Added 10 instead of 100.
Added 1000 instead of 100.
Went 100 LESS instead of 100 more.

question.explanation: 3950 + 100: the 9 hundreds become 10 hundreds, which roll over into a new thousand — 4050.

micros.title: Lining Up the Columns
micros.description: Numbers of different lengths must be lined up from the RIGHT, ones under ones — like books pushed to the right end of a shelf. Then add column by column without regrouping.
outcomes: Can set out a 3-digit and a 2-digit number with the ones aligned
Can add 3-digit numbers column by column when no carrying is needed

question.prompt: What is 345 + 62?

options.diagnosis: Lined the numbers up from the left, turning 62 into 620.
Forgot to carry when 4 tens + 6 tens made 10 tens.
Subtracted instead of adding.

question.explanation: Line up the ones: 5 + 2 = 7 ones; 4 + 6 = 10 tens — write 0, carry 1 hundred; 3 + 1 = 4 hundreds. Answer: 407.

micros.title: Adding with Carrying
micros.description: When a column's total reaches 10, bundle it and carry into the next column. Carries can travel from ones to tens and from tens to hundreds in the same sum.
outcomes: Can add two 3-digit numbers with one or two carries
Can say aloud what each carry stands for

question.prompt: What is 456 + 378?

options.diagnosis: Forgot to carry the ten from 6 + 8 = 14 into the tens column.
Forgot to carry the hundred from the tens column into the hundreds.
Subtracted instead of adding.

question.explanation: Ones: 6 + 8 = 14 — write 4, carry 1. Tens: 5 + 7 + 1 = 13 — write 3, carry 1. Hundreds: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Answer: 834.

micros.title: Subtracting with Borrowing
micros.description: When a column's top digit is too small, open a bundle from the next column: one ten becomes ten ones. The top number is the starting amount — order matters, so never just flip the digits.
outcomes: Can subtract 3-digit numbers borrowing from tens and hundreds
Can explain a borrow as opening a ten or a hundred

question.prompt: What is 624 − 357?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in every column instead of borrowing.
Borrowed for the ones but forgot to cross out one ten.
Added instead of subtracting.

question.explanation: Ones: 14 − 7 = 7. Tens: 11 − 5 = 6. Hundreds: 5 − 3 = 2. Answer: 267. Check by adding back: 267 + 357 = 624. ✓

micros.title: Borrowing Across a Zero
micros.description: When the top number has a 0 in the middle, rename before subtracting: 403 becomes 3 hundreds + 9 tens + 13 ones. Write the renamed number fully, THEN subtract column by column.
outcomes: Can subtract when the top number has a zero in the tens or ones place
Can rename a number like 403 or 500 before subtracting

question.prompt: What is 403 − 187?

options.diagnosis: Borrowed through the zero but never reduced the 4 hundreds to 3.
Skipped the zero while borrowing instead of opening a hundred into tens.
Took the smaller digit from the larger in every column — no borrowing at all.

question.explanation: Rename 403 as 3 hundreds + 9 tens + 13 ones. Ones: 13 − 7 = 6. Tens: 9 − 8 = 1. Hundreds: 3 − 1 = 2. Answer: 216.

micros.title: Estimating First and Checking Back
micros.description: Round each number to the nearest hundred and add or subtract in your head to know roughly what to expect — wild answers get caught. Check any subtraction by adding back.
outcomes: Can estimate a sum or difference to the nearest hundred before computing
Can check a subtraction by adding the answer to the number taken away

question.prompt: Which is the best ESTIMATE for 498 + 305, to the nearest hundred?

options.diagnosis: Rounded 498 down to 400 — but 498 is much nearer to 500.
Rounded 305 up to 400 — but 305 is much nearer to 300.
That is the exact answer, not an estimate — estimating uses round numbers.

question.explanation: 498 is close to 500 and 305 is close to 300, so the sum is about 500 + 300 = 800. The exact answer, 803, is right beside it.

micros.title: Story Problems with 3-digit Numbers
micros.description: Read the story, decide whether the pile grows (add) or shrinks (subtract), estimate, then compute. Words like 'sold', 'left' and 'in all' are the clues.
outcomes: Can choose the right operation from a story
Can solve add and subtract stories with 3-digit numbers and check the answer is sensible

micros.title: From Equal Groups to Table Facts
micros.description: Every table fact is an equal-groups story and an array picture: 3 × 4 is 3 plates of 4 laddoos. Group stories also settle the special cases — any number of empty plates gives 0, and plates of 1 give exactly the number of plates.
outcomes: Can turn an equal-groups picture or story into a multiplication fact
Can explain why n × 0 = 0 and n × 1 = n with a group story

question.prompt: There are 7 plates with 0 biscuits on each plate. How many biscuits in all?

options.diagnosis: Treated × 0 like + 0, which changes nothing — but 7 empty plates hold nothing.
Wrote a zero after the 7 — that is multiplying by 10, not by 0.
Treated multiplying like adding one more.

question.explanation: 7 × 0 means 7 plates with NOTHING on each: 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0. Any number times zero is zero.

micros.title: Tables of 2, 5 and 10
micros.description: The friendliest tables first: 2s are doubles, 5s end in 5 or 0, 10s just gain a zero. Skip counting and quick-fire recall make these facts automatic.
outcomes: Can recall the 2, 5 and 10 times tables in and out of order
Can spot the ending-digit patterns of the 5s and 10s

question.prompt: What is 5 × 6?

options.diagnosis: Slipped to the neighbouring fact 5 × 5 = 25.
Slipped to the neighbouring fact 5 × 7 = 35.
Added 5 + 6 instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: Skip count in fives six times: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. So 5 × 6 = 30 — fives always end in 5 or 0.

micros.title: Tables of 3, 4 and 6
micros.description: Build the 3s by adding a group to the 2s, the 4s by doubling the 2s, and the 6s by doubling the 3s. Deriving from a known fact beats guessing.
outcomes: Can recall the 3, 4 and 6 times tables
Can derive a 4s or 6s fact by doubling a known fact

question.prompt: What is 6 × 4?

options.diagnosis: Slipped to the neighbouring fact 5 × 4 = 20.
Slipped to the neighbouring fact 7 × 4 = 28.
Added 6 + 4 instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: Double a known fact: 3 × 4 = 12, so 6 × 4 = 12 + 12 = 24.

micros.title: Tables of 7, 8 and 9
micros.description: The trickiest facts live here. Anchor and derive: from 7 × 7 = 49 get 7 × 8 = 56; get the 9s from the 10s by taking one group away. Drill the few slippery facts separately.
outcomes: Can recall the 7, 8 and 9 times tables
Can derive a hard fact from a nearby anchor fact

question.prompt: What is 9 × 6?

options.diagnosis: Slipped to the neighbouring fact 8 × 6 = 48.
Slipped to the neighbouring fact 9 × 5 = 45.
Added 9 + 6 instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: Use the 10s as an anchor: 10 × 6 = 60, take away one 6 → 9 × 6 = 54.

micros.title: Turn-around Facts and Missing Factors
micros.description: Rotating an array a quarter turn shows a × b = b × a — every fact you learn gives its twin for free. Fact families also answer missing-factor puzzles like 6 × __ = 42.
outcomes: Can use the turn-around rule a × b = b × a
Can find the missing factor in facts like 6 × __ = 42

question.prompt: Meera knows 8 × 3 = 24. Now she needs 3 × 8. What should she do?

options.text: Nothing new — it is the same total, 24; order does not matter in multiplication
Count again from the start — the answer might be different
Add one: 3 × 8 must be 25
options.diagnosis: Thinks swapping the factors changes the total slightly.

options.text: Add the numbers: 3 × 8 = 11
options.diagnosis: Fell back to addition under uncertainty.

question.explanation: An 8-row, 3-column array turned sideways becomes 3 rows of 8 — same dots, same total. So 3 × 8 = 8 × 3 = 24.

micros.title: Splitting into Tens and Ones
micros.description: To multiply 14 × 2, split 14 into 10 and 4 and multiply BOTH parts: (10 × 2) + (4 × 2). Both parts get the same operation — times, never add.
outcomes: Can split a 2-digit number into tens and ones for multiplying
Can multiply both parts and add them, without mixing in addition

question.prompt: What is 14 × 2?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied only the ones (4 × 2 = 8) and copied the tens digit unchanged.
Multiplied the ones but ADDED the tens digit to 2 (1 + 2 = 3).
Added 14 + 2 instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: Split by place value: 14 × 2 = (10 × 2) + (4 × 2) = 20 + 8 = 28. Both parts of 14 get multiplied by 2.

micros.title: Area Model: Add the Partial Products
micros.description: Draw the number as a rectangle cut into a tens box and a ones box, work out each box, then ADD the parts. The parts combine by addition — never by sitting side by side.
outcomes: Can find both partial products with an area model
Can combine partial products by adding, not gluing digits together

question.prompt: What is 26 × 3?

options.diagnosis: Wrote the partial answers 6 and 18 side by side instead of adding 60 + 18.
The carried ten from 6 × 3 = 18 was written but never added.
Added 26 + 3 instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: Two boxes: 20 × 3 = 60 and 6 × 3 = 18. ADD the parts: 60 + 18 = 78.

micros.title: Column Method with Carrying
micros.description: The short written form of the area model: multiply the ones, carry the extra tens, multiply the tens, THEN add the carry. Say it aloud and cross out each carry once it is used.
outcomes: Can multiply a 2-digit number by a 1-digit number in columns with carrying
Can say the multiply-then-add-the-carry ritual aloud

question.prompt: What is 58 × 3?

options.diagnosis: Forgot to add the carried 2: 5 × 3 = 15, plus the carry makes 17.
Glued the partial products 15 and 24 side by side.
Added 58 + 3 instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: Ones: 8 × 3 = 24 — write 4, carry 2. Tens: 5 × 3 = 15, plus the carried 2 = 17. Answer: 174. Estimate check: about 60 × 3 = 180. ✓

micros.title: Estimating Products
micros.description: Round the 2-digit number to the nearest ten and multiply in your head: 62 × 4 is about 60 × 4 = 240. The estimate flags answers that are far too big or too small.
outcomes: Can estimate a product by rounding to the nearest ten
Can use the estimate to judge whether a computed answer is sensible

question.prompt: Which is the best ESTIMATE for 62 × 4?

options.diagnosis: Estimated 6 × 4 and lost the tens — 62 is about 60, not 6.
An extra zero slipped in — 60 × 4 is 240, not 2400.
Added 62 + 4 instead of multiplying.

question.explanation: 62 is close to 60, and 60 × 4 = 240. The exact answer, 248, sits right beside the estimate.

micros.title: Equal-groups Story Problems
micros.description: Spot the equal groups in a story — boxes of pencils, tickets at the same price — write the multiplication, estimate, then compute.
outcomes: Can turn an equal-groups story into a 2-digit by 1-digit multiplication
Can solve and check the answer against an estimate

question.prompt: One box holds 24 pencils. How many pencils are in 3 boxes?

options.diagnosis: Added 24 + 3 instead of multiplying.
Wrote the partial products 6 and 12 side by side.
Dropped the carry: 4 × 3 = 12, the carried ten never got added.

question.explanation: 24 × 3 = (20 × 3) + (4 × 3) = 60 + 12 = 72 pencils. Estimate check: about 20 × 3 = 60, so 72 is sensible.

micros.title: Division as Sharing
micros.description: Share 15 mangoes among 3 friends by dealing them out one round at a time like playing cards, then count ONE friend's pile. The answer is how many EACH gets, with its unit.
outcomes: Can solve sharing problems by dealing out objects or drawing
Can state the answer with its unit: '5 mangoes EACH'

question.prompt: 15 mangoes are shared equally among 3 friends. How many mangoes does each friend get?

options.diagnosis: Echoed the number of friends instead of finding each friend's share.
Multiplied 15 × 3 instead of dividing.
Subtracted 15 − 3 instead of dividing.

question.explanation: Deal them out: 1 each, then another, until all 15 are gone — each friend has 5. Check: 3 × 5 = 15. ✓

micros.title: Division as Grouping
micros.description: The other division question: 20 rotis, 5 per box — how many BOXES? Make groups of the given size and count the groups, or subtract 5 again and again.
outcomes: Can solve grouping problems by making groups of a given size
Can tell a sharing question from a grouping question

micros.title: Writing Division Sentences
micros.description: Write and read sentences like 15 ÷ 3 = 5. The order tells the story: the first number is what gets shared, the second is how it is shared — swapping them changes everything.
outcomes: Can write a division sentence for a sharing or grouping story
Can explain why 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 are different

question.prompt: Is 10 ÷ 2 the same as 2 ÷ 10?

options.text: No — sharing 10 among 2 is a different story from sharing 2 among 10
Yes — just like 2 + 10 = 10 + 2
Yes — order never matters in maths
No — because 2 ÷ 10 is 5
options.diagnosis: Right answer, wrong reason: computed 10 ÷ 2 anyway, ignoring the order.

question.explanation: 10 ÷ 2 = 5: two children get 5 each. But 2 ÷ 10 shares just 2 things among 10 children — not even one each! Order matters in division.

micros.title: Division from Multiplication Facts
micros.description: Division is multiplication run backwards: to find 42 ÷ 6, ask '6 times WHAT makes 42?'. Every table fact gives two divisions for free.
outcomes: Can solve a division using a known multiplication fact
Can write the fact family for a triple like 6, 7, 42

question.prompt: Use a table fact: what is 42 ÷ 6?

options.diagnosis: Echoed the divisor instead of asking '6 times what makes 42?'.
Table slip: 6 × 8 = 48, not 42.
Subtracted 42 − 6 instead of dividing.

question.explanation: Ask: 6 × ? = 42. From the tables, 6 × 7 = 42, so 42 ÷ 6 = 7.

micros.title: Leftovers: Simple Remainders
micros.description: Sometimes things do not share out evenly — what is left goes in the 'remainder dish' and must ALWAYS be reported: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2.
outcomes: Can share with a leftover and report both parts of the answer
Can say what could happen to the leftover in a story

question.prompt: 17 pencils are shared equally among 5 children. What happens?

options.text: Each gets 3 pencils, and 2 pencils are left over
Each gets 3 pencils, nothing is left
options.diagnosis: 5 × 3 = 15, but there were 17 — two pencils vanished!

options.text: Each gets 4 pencils
options.diagnosis: 5 × 4 = 20 — that is more pencils than we have.

options.text: They cannot be shared at all
options.diagnosis: Division still works when sharing is not exact — report the remainder.

question.explanation: 5 children × 3 pencils = 15 used, and 17 − 15 = 2 remain. We say 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2. The leftover must always be reported!

micros.title: Equal Parts: The Fairness Test
micros.description: Fraction parts must be EQUAL — a big piece and a small piece are not halves. Test with fairness: would both children happily take either piece? Fold and stack paper shapes to check parts match.
outcomes: Can fold or cut a shape into equal parts and check by stacking
Can reject unequal cuts as 'not halves / not thirds'

question.prompt: Meena cuts a paper into 3 pieces — two big ones and one tiny one. She says each piece is a third. Is she right?

options.text: No — thirds must be 3 EQUAL pieces
Yes — 3 pieces always means 3 thirds
Yes — any piece of the paper is a third
No — paper cannot be cut into thirds
options.diagnosis: Over-corrected: it can, but only with equal pieces.

question.explanation: Cutting into 3 pieces is not enough — thirds must be equal. Try the fairness test: would three children happily take any piece? Only then are they true thirds.

micros.title: Naming Halves and Quarters
micros.description: A half is ONE out of 2 equal parts, a quarter is ONE out of 4. Say 'one out of 4 equal parts' while pointing at a real cut shape, then write it as 1/2 or 1/4.
outcomes: Can name and write 1/2 and 1/4 for one part of an equally divided whole
Can read 1/4 as 'one out of 4 equal parts', not as two separate numbers

question.prompt: What does 1/4 mean?

options.text: One out of 4 equal parts of a whole
The numbers 1 and 4 written together
One whole and four more
options.diagnosis: Read the top and bottom as unrelated counts of wholes.

options.text: Four equal parts out of one
options.diagnosis: Swapped the top and bottom — the 4 below says how many parts the whole is cut into.

question.explanation: The bottom number says the whole is cut into 4 EQUAL parts; the top says we take 1 of them. So 1/4 is one out of 4 equal parts — a quarter.

micros.title: Thirds
micros.description: Cut or fold a whole into 3 equal parts: each part is one third, written 1/3. Folding into three takes more care than halving — fold, check, adjust.
outcomes: Can fold or mark a shape into 3 equal parts
Can name and write 1/3 for one of 3 equal parts

micros.title: Comparing Halves, Thirds and Quarters
micros.description: Of the SAME whole, 1/2 beats 1/3, and 1/3 beats 1/4 — more cuts mean smaller pieces. Lay folded pieces on top of each other to see it.
outcomes: Can explain why 1/2 of a whole is bigger than 1/3 or 1/4 of the same whole
Can order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 by size

question.prompt: You may take 1/2 or 1/3 of the SAME roti. Which piece is bigger?

options.text: 1/3 — because 3 is bigger than 2
They are the same size
options.diagnosis: Both are 'one piece', but a roti cut in 2 gives bigger pieces than one cut in 3.

options.text: You cannot compare them
options.diagnosis: Saw only unrelated whole numbers, not shares of the same roti.

question.explanation: Cutting into 2 parts gives big pieces; cutting into 3 gives smaller ones. So 1/2 > 1/3. More pieces means smaller pieces!

micros.title: Half or Quarter of a Collection
micros.description: Fractions work on groups too: half of 8 mangoes means splitting the 8 into 2 equal piles — 4 each. A quarter means 4 equal piles.
outcomes: Can find half of a small even collection
Can find a quarter of a collection that splits into 4 equal piles

question.prompt: What is HALF of 8 mangoes?

options.diagnosis: Doubled instead of halving.
Found a quarter (4 piles) instead of a half (2 piles).
Took one away — half means splitting into 2 EQUAL piles.

question.explanation: Split 8 mangoes into 2 equal piles: 4 and 4. Half of 8 is 4.

micros.title: Rupees and Paise
micros.description: 100 paise make ₹1 — paise are not rupees! Write mixed amounts with a dot, like ₹7.50, and keep rupees and paise in their own columns on a money mat.
outcomes: Can state that ₹1 = 100 paise
Can write an amount like 7 rupees 50 paise as ₹7.50

question.prompt: How do we write 7 rupees and 50 paise?

options.diagnosis: Added the 50 paise straight into the rupees — paise are hundredths of a rupee.
Wrote the paise as if they were rupees.
Added 7 + 5, mixing up the numbers entirely.

question.explanation: Rupees before the dot, paise after: ₹7.50. Since 100 paise = ₹1, 50 paise is only half a rupee — never 50 whole rupees.

micros.title: Adding Amounts of Money
micros.description: Add prices the same way as 3-digit numbers — line up, add, carry — and write the ₹ sign on the answer. This is how a shop bill total is made.
outcomes: Can add two or three money amounts in rupees
Can total a simple bill

question.prompt: Ravi buys a car toy for ₹56 and a kite for ₹27. How much does he spend in all?

options.diagnosis: Forgot to carry the ten from 6 + 7 = 13.
Wrote the 13 ones without regrouping into a ten.
Subtracted the prices instead of adding them.

question.explanation: ₹56 + ₹27: ones 6 + 7 = 13 — write 3, carry 1. Tens: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8. Total: ₹83.

micros.title: Finding Change by Counting Up
micros.description: Change is what comes BACK: count up from the price to the note on a number line — 42 → 50 is 8, then 50 → 100 is 50 more. Change is always found by subtracting, never adding.
outcomes: Can find change from ₹50 or ₹100 by counting up
Can check change by adding it back to the price

question.prompt: A pencil box costs ₹42. You pay with a ₹100 note. How much change should you get?

options.diagnosis: Added the price and the payment — but change comes BACK, so it must be less than ₹100.
Counted up only to ₹90 — go all the way to ₹100.
Counting-up slip: 42 to 50 is ₹8, not ₹2.

question.explanation: Count up: 42 → 50 is ₹8, then 50 → 100 is ₹50; 8 + 50 = ₹58. Check: ₹58 is less than the ₹100 handed over. ✓

micros.title: Bills with Quantities: Multiply, Don't Add
micros.description: When a bill line says 3 pencils at ₹12 each, the quantity MULTIPLIES the price: 3 × 12 = 36. Write the line as repeated addition first, then compress it to a multiplication.
outcomes: Can compute a bill line as quantity × price
Can total a bill with one multiplied line and one single item

question.prompt: Bill: 3 pencils at ₹12 each, and 1 rubber for ₹8. What is the total?

options.diagnosis: Added 12 + 3 + 8 — the quantity must MULTIPLY the price.
Charged for only one pencil — forgot the quantity 3.
Charged for four pencils (48) — one 12 too many.

question.explanation: Pencils: 3 × ₹12 = ₹36. Rubber: ₹8. Total: 36 + 8 = ₹44.

micros.title: Is the Answer Sensible?
micros.description: Install the sanity checks: change must be LESS than what you handed over, and a bill total should match a quick estimate. Catch silly answers before the shopkeeper does.
outcomes: Can judge whether a total or change is reasonable without full computing
Can state the rule: change is always smaller than the payment

question.prompt: A toy costs ₹67. You pay with a ₹100 note. A friend says your change is ₹167. WITHOUT working out the sum, how do you know that is wrong?

options.text: Change must be smaller than the ₹100 you handed over
It is not wrong — you add the price and the payment to get change
It is wrong because change should always be exactly ₹100
options.diagnosis: Change is the payment MINUS the price — it depends on the price.

options.text: You cannot know without working out the whole sum
options.diagnosis: Sanity checks work without computing: money back can never beat money given.

question.explanation: You gave ₹100, so at most ₹100 can come back — ₹167 is impossible. (The real change is 100 − 67 = ₹33.)

micros.title: Straight and Curved Lines
micros.description: Straight means 'does not bend' — direction does not matter, so slanted and standing lines are just as straight as lying ones. Test with a taut string or a ruler's edge.
outcomes: Can sort lines and edges into straight and curved
Can accept slanted and vertical lines as straight

question.prompt: Which of these is a STRAIGHT line?

options.text: A tightly stretched kite string, even though it slants
The rim of a round bangle
options.diagnosis: The rim curves all the way round — it bends, so it is not straight.

options.text: A bent straw
options.diagnosis: Bent means not straight, even if parts of it look straight.

options.text: None of these — a slanting line is not straight

question.explanation: Straight means it does not bend — slanting is fine! A taut string is straight whichever way it leans.

micros.title: Counting Sides and Corners
micros.description: A polygon's sides are its straight edges and its corners are where two sides meet. Counting sides and corners — not squinting at the look — is how shapes get their names.
outcomes: Can count the sides and corners of triangles, rectangles and other polygons
Can name a shape from its side and corner count

micros.title: A Shape Keeps Its Name When Turned
micros.description: Rotate a cut-out slowly and recount: 4 equal sides and 4 square corners is a square in ANY position. Turning a shape never changes what it is.
outcomes: Can recognise squares, triangles and rectangles in any orientation
Can justify a shape's name by counting, not by how it sits

question.prompt: Ali turns a triangle cut-out so its point faces down. What shape is it now?

options.text: Still a triangle — it still has 3 sides and 3 corners
It is not a triangle any more — triangles point up
A diamond
options.diagnosis: Renamed the shape because of how it sits — count the sides instead.

options.text: A cone
options.diagnosis: A cone is a solid 3D shape; this is a flat cut-out.

question.explanation: Count, don't just look: 3 sides, 3 corners — a triangle, whichever way it points. Turning a shape never changes its name.

micros.title: Composing Shapes: Tangram Play
micros.description: The same pieces can build different shapes depending on which edges meet. Predict first, then test: two equal triangles can make a square, a rectangle or a bigger triangle.
outcomes: Can compose new shapes from tangram-style pieces
Can predict what two given shapes will make before joining them

question.prompt: Sara cuts a rectangle along its diagonal and gets 2 equal triangles. What can she make by joining them edge to edge?

options.text: The rectangle again, or a bigger triangle — depending on which edges she joins
Only a bigger triangle
Nothing new — triangles cannot make other shapes
A circle
options.diagnosis: Straight-edged pieces can never make a curved shape.

question.explanation: Join the two longest edges to get the rectangle back; join two matching short edges to get a bigger triangle. Same pieces, different joins, different shapes!

micros.title: Measuring with a Ruler from 0
micros.description: Line the object's end up with the 0 mark — not the ruler's edge — and read where the other end lands. Length counts the SPACES between marks, not the marks themselves.
outcomes: Can measure an object in cm starting from the 0 mark
Can explain that length counts gaps, not marks

micros.title: Broken-Ruler Measuring
micros.description: When an object does not start at 0, subtract: length = end mark − start mark. Measure the same pencil from 0 and from 1 and see why both readings agree.
outcomes: Can measure correctly when the object starts at any mark
Can find a length by subtracting the start mark from the end mark

question.prompt: An eraser lies along a ruler from the 2 cm mark to the 7 cm mark. How long is the eraser?

options.text: 5 cm
7 cm
options.diagnosis: Read only the finishing mark, ignoring that the eraser starts at 2.

options.text: 2 cm
options.diagnosis: Read the starting mark instead of the length.

options.text: 9 cm
options.diagnosis: Added the two marks instead of subtracting.

question.explanation: Length is the gap between the ends: 7 − 2 = 5 cm. Starting at 0 is handy, but any start works if you subtract.

micros.title: Metres and Centimetres: 1 m = 100 cm
micros.description: Unroll a metre tape and count the centimetres in tens: 10, 20, ... 100. Exactly 100 cm make 1 m, so 2 m = 200 cm — always two zeros, never one.
outcomes: Can state that 1 m = 100 cm
Can convert whole metres to centimetres

question.prompt: 2 metres = how many centimetres?

options.diagnosis: Used 1 m = 10 cm — but a metre holds one HUNDRED centimetres.
Mixed up with 1 km = 1000 m (or 1 kg = 1000 g).
Added 100 + 2 instead of taking 2 lots of 100.

question.explanation: Each metre is 100 cm, so 2 m = 2 × 100 = 200 cm.

micros.title: Estimating and Choosing cm or m
micros.description: Build body benchmarks — a fingernail is about 1 cm, a giant step about 1 m — then estimate before measuring and pick the sensible unit. Always say the unit with the number.
outcomes: Can pick cm or m sensibly for an object
Can estimate a length using body benchmarks before measuring

question.prompt: Which is the best estimate for the length of your maths book?

options.text: 25 centimetres
25 metres
options.diagnosis: That is longer than a classroom — the unit was ignored.

options.text: 2 centimetres
options.diagnosis: About the width of a finger — far too short for a book.

options.text: 1 metre
options.diagnosis: That is a giant step long — books are much shorter; use the fingernail benchmark.

question.explanation: A maths book is about 25 fingernail-widths long — 25 cm. Benchmarks (fingernail ≈ 1 cm, giant step ≈ 1 m) keep estimates sensible.

micros.title: Heavier or Lighter: Trust the Balance
micros.description: Big does not mean heavy and tall does not mean holds-more. Predict, then test on a balance or by pouring — let the measurement, not the look, give the answer.
outcomes: Can compare weights with a balance and capacities by pouring
Can give examples where the bigger-looking thing is lighter

question.prompt: A BIG bag of puffed rice and a SMALL brick sit on the two pans of a balance. The brick's pan goes down. Which is heavier?

options.text: The brick — the pan that goes down holds the heavier thing
The bag — it is much bigger
They weigh the same
options.diagnosis: A level balance means equal — this one tilted.

options.text: You cannot tell without weighing them
options.diagnosis: The balance IS the weighing — it already gave the answer.

question.explanation: The balance tells the truth: the brick's pan sank, so the small brick is heavier than the big fluffy bag. Big is not the same as heavy!

micros.title: Grams and Kilograms: 1 kg = 1000 g
micros.description: Kilo means one thousand: stack ten 100 g packets and you have exactly 1 kg. Converting kg to g always uses 1000, never 100.
outcomes: Can state that 1 kg = 1000 g
Can convert whole kilograms to grams

question.prompt: 2 kilograms = how many grams?

options.diagnosis: Used 1 kg = 100 g — but kilo means one THOUSAND.
The kilo step is a thousand, not ten.
Added 1000 + 2 instead of taking 2 lots of 1000.

question.explanation: Each kilogram is 1000 g, so 2 kg = 2 × 1000 = 2000 g.

micros.title: Millilitres and Litres: 1 L = 1000 mL
micros.description: Liquids are measured in millilitres and litres: five 200 mL cups fill a 1 L bottle. Convert to the SAME unit before comparing any two amounts.
outcomes: Can state that 1 L = 1000 mL
Can compare two amounts by converting to the same unit first

question.prompt: Which is more: 750 mL or 1 L?

options.text: 1 L — because 1 L is 1000 mL, and 1000 is more than 750
750 mL — because 750 is bigger than 1
options.diagnosis: Compared the numbers while ignoring the units.

options.text: They are the same
options.diagnosis: Guessed equality without converting to the same unit.

options.text: You cannot compare a mL amount with a L amount
options.diagnosis: You can — convert them to the same unit first.

question.explanation: Convert first: 1 L = 1000 mL. Now compare: 1000 mL > 750 mL, so 1 L is more.

micros.title: Choosing Sensible Units
micros.description: Pick g for light things and kg for heavy ones, mL for spoonfuls and L for buckets — but remember the unit measures the AMOUNT, not the material: 1 kg of cotton equals 1 kg of iron.
outcomes: Can choose g/kg and mL/L sensibly for everyday things
Can explain that same number + same unit = same amount, whatever the stuff

question.prompt: Rahim says: 'You cannot weigh cotton in kilograms — kg is only for heavy things like iron.' Is he right?

options.text: No — 1 kg of cotton weighs exactly as much as 1 kg of iron; kg measures any amount
Yes — light materials can only be weighed in grams
Yes — a kilogram of cotton is lighter than a kilogram of iron
options.diagnosis: Judged by the material's reputation, not the measured amount.

options.text: No — but only if the cotton is squeezed into a small ball
options.diagnosis: Weight does not change with size or squashing — the balance stays level either way.

question.explanation: Put a weighed 1 kg cotton bundle and a 1 kg iron block on a balance — they level exactly. Units belong to amounts, not to materials.

micros.title: Comparing and Adding Weights and Capacities
micros.description: Add and compare weights or capacities once they are in the same unit: 500 g + 250 g = 750 g; a 500 mL bottle and a 500 mL mug together fill a 1 L jug.
outcomes: Can add simple weights or capacities given in the same unit
Can solve simple shopping and pouring comparisons

micros.title: The Jobs of the Two Hands
micros.description: Sort the hands' jobs aloud before every read: SHORT hand tells the hour, LONG hand tells the minutes. Start with o'clock times where the long hand rests on 12.
outcomes: Can identify the hour hand and minute hand
Can read o'clock times correctly

question.prompt: The LONG hand points to 12 and the SHORT hand points to 9. What time is it?

options.text: 9 o'clock

options.diagnosis: Swapped the hands — took the long hand for the hour and the short hand for the minutes.
Read the long hand's 12 as 12 minutes; on 12 it means zero minutes — o'clock.

options.text: 12 o'clock
options.diagnosis: Read the long hand as the hour hand.

question.explanation: Short hand = hour: 9. Long hand on 12 = zero minutes past. So it is exactly 9 o'clock.

micros.title: Counting Minutes in Fives
micros.description: For the long hand, each clock number is worth 5 minutes: chant round from 12 — 5, 10, 15 ... 55. The number the long hand touches is NOT its face value.
outcomes: Can count minutes in fives around the clock face
Can say how many minutes past when the long hand is on any number

question.prompt: The long (minute) hand points to 8. How many minutes past the hour is it?

options.text: 40 minutes
8 minutes
options.diagnosis: Read the 8 at face value — each number is worth 5 minutes.

options.text: 45 minutes
options.diagnosis: Counted one number too far — 45 belongs to the 9.

options.text: 20 minutes
options.diagnosis: That is the 4 — count in fives all the way round: 5, 10, ... 40.

question.explanation: Count in fives from 12: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40. On the 8, it is 40 minutes past the hour.

micros.title: Half Past and Quarter Past
micros.description: Half past means the long hand on 6 (30 minutes); quarter past means it on 3 (15 minutes). Meanwhile the hour hand creeps: at half past 7 it floats between 7 and 8 — but the hour is still 7.
outcomes: Can read times to the half and quarter hour
Can name the hour from a hand sitting between two numbers

question.prompt: The SHORT hand is halfway between 7 and 8, and the LONG hand points to 6. What time is it?

options.text: Half past 7
Half past 8
options.diagnosis: Read the hour hand at the number it is approaching — the hour is the number it has PASSED.
Read the long hand's 6 at face value; on 6 it means 30 minutes.

options.text: 6 o'clock
options.diagnosis: Took the long hand for the hour hand.

question.explanation: Long hand on 6 = 30 minutes past. The short hand has left 7 but not reached 8, so the hour is still 7. Time: half past 7 (7:30).

micros.title: Reading Time to 5 Minutes
micros.description: Put it all together: hour from the short hand's last-passed number, minutes by counting the long hand's fives — 11:20, 3:45, 6:05.
outcomes: Can read any time to the nearest 5 minutes
Can write clock times in hh:mm form

question.prompt: The LONG hand points to 4 and the SHORT hand is a little past 11. What time is it?

options.diagnosis: Read the long hand's 4 at face value — on 4 it means 20 minutes.
The short hand is only APPROACHING 12; the hour is the 11 it has passed.
Swapped the hands' jobs.

question.explanation: Short hand: just past 11, so the hour is 11. Long hand on 4: count 5, 10, 15, 20. Time: 11:20.

micros.title: Calendar: Days Between Dates
micros.description: Use the calendar to count days between two dates in the same month: count from tomorrow up to the target day, or subtract the dates.
outcomes: Can find how many days between two dates in a month
Can read dates, days and months from a calendar page

question.prompt: Sports day is on 21 November. Today is 14 November. How many days are left until sports day?

options.diagnosis: Counted today as a waiting day as well as the 21st.
Stopped counting one day early — count 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21.
Added the two dates instead of finding the gap.

question.explanation: Count from tomorrow: 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21 — that is 7 days. Or subtract: 21 − 14 = 7.

micros.title: Skip Counting by 2s, 5s and 10s
micros.description: Make equal jumps on the number line starting from the jump number: 2, 4, 6...; 5, 10, 15...; 10, 20, 30... Spot the ending-digit patterns each family makes.
outcomes: Can skip count by 2s, 5s and 10s from their own multiples
Can describe the ending-digit pattern of each count

micros.title: Skip Counting from Any Start
micros.description: The rule of a skip pattern is the JUMP SIZE — the starting stone is free. Jumping +5 from 3 lands on 3, 8, 13, 18, and that is a perfectly good pattern.
outcomes: Can continue a skip pattern that starts away from the skip number
Can state a pattern's jump size from its first few terms

question.prompt: A pattern goes 3, 8, 13, 18, ... What comes next?

options.text: Nothing — counting by 5s must go 5, 10, 15

options.diagnosis: Added 1 instead of the pattern's jump of 5.
Jumped 6 — check the earlier jumps: each one is exactly 5.

question.explanation: Every jump is +5: 3 → 8 → 13 → 18 → 23. Skip counting can start anywhere — the rule is the jump, not the starting number.

micros.title: Even and Odd by Pairing
micros.description: A number is even if its counters all pair up with none left over, and odd if one is left alone. Numbers ending in 0 pair up perfectly too — they are even.
outcomes: Can decide even or odd by pairing up counters
Can show that numbers like 30 are even because nothing is left over

question.prompt: Pair up 30 counters, two by two. What happens — and is 30 even or odd?

options.text: Every counter finds a partner, none left over — 30 is EVEN
30 is neither even nor odd — it ends in nothing
One counter is left alone — 30 is odd
options.diagnosis: Try it: 15 pairs form and nothing is left over.

options.text: You cannot pair up such a big number
options.diagnosis: Pairing works for any number — and the ones digit gives a shortcut.

question.explanation: 30 counters make exactly 15 pairs with none left over, so 30 is even. Even endings are 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 — zero belongs on the list!

micros.title: The Ones-Digit Shortcut
micros.description: Only the ONES digit decides even or odd, because tens and hundreds always split into pairs. 21 is odd since 1 is odd — the 2 in front has no say.
outcomes: Can decide even or odd for any 2- or 3-digit number using the ones digit
Can explain why the other digits do not matter

question.prompt: Is 21 even or odd — and why?

options.text: Odd, because the ones digit 1 is odd — one counter would be left without a pair
Even, because it starts with 2
Even, because 21 can be split into two parts
options.diagnosis: Any number splits into two parts; even needs two EQUAL parts with none left over.

options.text: Neither — some numbers are in between
options.diagnosis: Every whole number is exactly one of even or odd.

question.explanation: The 2 tens make 10 pairs by themselves, so only the ones digit decides: 1 is odd, so 21 is odd.

micros.title: Describing and Extending Pattern Rules
micros.description: Say the rule out loud — 'add 10 each time', 'the numbers go even, odd, even, odd' — then use it to extend the pattern and to invent new patterns of your own.
outcomes: Can state the rule of a number pattern in words
Can extend a pattern by its rule and make up a new pattern from a given rule

micros.title: Tally Marks and Tables
micros.description: Record counts as tally marks in bundles of five — four sticks and a gate — and line the totals up in a neat table of rows and columns.
outcomes: Can record a count with tally marks in fives
Can fill and read a simple data table

micros.title: Reading a Bar Chart
micros.description: Follow a bar's top across to the scale to read its value, and answer questions from what the CHART says — point to the bar that proves your answer, not to your favourite.
outcomes: Can read values from a simple bar chart
Can answer most/least questions using the chart as evidence

question.prompt: A chart of favourite fruits shows: Mango 9, Apple 5, Banana 7. Which fruit did the MOST children choose?

options.text: Mango — its bar is the tallest, at 9
Apple — apples are everyone's favourite
options.diagnosis: Answered from opinion — the chart says only 5 chose apple.

options.text: Banana
options.diagnosis: Second tallest — compare all the bars before choosing.

options.text: You cannot tell from a chart
options.diagnosis: The chart is exactly the evidence — follow the tallest bar.

question.explanation: Compare the bars: 9 > 7 > 5. The mango bar is tallest, so mango was chosen most. Always answer from the chart, not from memory!

micros.title: When One Step Stands for 2
micros.description: Check the scale BEFORE reading any bar: when one step stands for 2 or more, multiply the steps by the scale — never just count steps as ones.
outcomes: Can read a bar chart whose scale is 2 or more per step
Can explain why the scale must be read first

question.prompt: In a bar chart, each step on the scale stands for 2 children. The 'milk' bar is 5 steps tall. How many children does it show?

options.diagnosis: Counted the steps but ignored the 2-per-step scale.
Added the scale to the steps (5 + 2) instead of multiplying.
Miscounted 6 steps before doubling — recount the steps.

question.explanation: Each step is worth 2, so 5 steps show 5 × 2 = 10 children. Read the scale before reading the bars!

micros.title: How Many More? Comparing Bars
micros.description: 'How many more' asks for a NUMBER, not a name: put a finger on the shorter bar's top and count the climb to the taller bar's top — that climb is the difference.
outcomes: Can answer how-many-more questions with a number found by subtracting
Can compare two categories from a chart or table

question.prompt: A chart shows how children come to school: Bus 14, Cycle 9. HOW MANY MORE children come by bus than by cycle?

options.text: Bus
options.diagnosis: Named the bigger category — but 'how many more' asks for a number.
Gave the bigger value itself instead of the difference.
Added the two values instead of finding the difference.

question.explanation: 'How many more' means find the difference: 14 − 9 = 5. Five more children come by bus than by cycle.

micros.title: Drawing a Bar Chart
micros.description: Turn a small table into a bar chart: label the categories, choose a scale, draw each bar to the right height with equal widths and equal gaps, and give the chart a title.
outcomes: Can draw a bar chart from a small table of data
Can choose and label a sensible scale
